title: DP on two strings
sub: LCS and Edit Distance: an (i, j) table over prefixes, three transitions, recovering the answer and O(min) memory
cards/0/title: LCS: the problem and the “two strings” signal
cards/0/body:
Longest Common Subsequence (LeetCode #1143). Given strings a and b of up to 1000 characters, find the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence is obtained by deleting characters without changing the order of the rest: “ace” is a subsequence of “abcde”, and “aec” is not. A substring, by contrast, is contiguous.

Naively — enumerate all 2ᵐ subsequences of a and check each one in b in O(n). With m = 1000 that is 2¹⁰⁰⁰ — pointless.

The signal of DP on two strings: two sequences, and the answer for the whole strings is built from answers for their prefixes — look at the last characters and cut off one or both. A subproblem is defined by a pair of lengths (i, j), and there are (m + 1)(n + 1) such pairs — about 10⁶ for m = n = 1000.

This signal identifies LCS, Edit Distance, pattern matching, Interleaving String and many others.
cards/1/q: What is the LCS length of “abcde” and “aec”?
cards/1/explain: The common characters are a, c, e, but order matters: in “abcde” c comes before e, and in “aec” after it. Together with a you can take either c (“ac”) or e (“ae”), but not both. The answer is 2.
cards/1/wrong/1: 3 would be the answer if order didn’t matter — that is the size of the intersection of the character sets. A subsequence keeps the order.
cards/1/wrong/2: One letter is too little: “ac” appears in both strings in order.
cards/2/body:
State: dp[i, j] is the LCS of the prefixes a[..i] and b[..j] (the first i and j characters). Base: an empty prefix — dp[0, j] = dp[i, 0] = 0. Answer: dp[m, n].

Transition — look at the last characters of the prefixes, a[i − 1] and b[j − 1]:

Equal — pair them up: dp[i − 1, j − 1] + 1 (the diagonal). This is safe: if an optimal LCS doesn’t use them, the last character of one of the strings in it can be swapped for this pair — the length won’t drop.
Different — at least one of them is not in the LCS. Cut either the character of a or the character of b: max(dp[i − 1, j], dp[i, j − 1]) — the maximum of the cell above and the cell to the left.

Order: rows top to bottom, left to right within a row — above, left and diagonal are all ready. Time O(m·n), memory O(m·n).
cards/2/flow/2: rows top to bottom, left to right
cards/3/explain: The table is shifted by one: dp[i, j] is about the first i characters, and the last of them is a[i − 1]. a[i] with i = a.Length would run past the string. A match adds a pair to the diagonal’s answer, a mismatch takes the better of the two ways to cut a character — the maximum, since we want the longest.
cards/4/task: Walk the LCS table for “abcde” and “ace”: rows are prefixes of abcde, columns are prefixes of ace. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes into a cell.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Cell (3, 2): “c” and “c”. Diagonal dp[2, 1] = 1, above dp[2, 2] = 1, left dp[3, 1] = 1. What goes in?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: The characters are equal — take the diagonal and add the pair: 1 + 1 = 2. That is “ac”: the “a” came from the diagonal, the “c” is the new pair. On a match we don’t look above or left.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: Cell (3, 3): “c” and “e”. Above dp[2, 3] = 1, left dp[3, 2] = 2, diagonal dp[2, 2] = 1. What goes in?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: The characters differ — the maximum of above and left: max(1, 2) = 2. Left is “abc” versus “ac”, which already has “ac”. Diagonal + 1 can’t be taken on a mismatch: there is no pair.
cards/5/title: Recover the answer and squeeze the memory
cards/5/body:
The LCS string itself. The table holds lengths, but you can walk it back from (m, n): characters equal — that is a character of the answer, go along the diagonal; otherwise go where the maximum came from — up or left. Characters are collected from the end, so reverse at the end. The walk back is O(m + n). That is how the answer is recovered in any DP: repeat the winning transition.

O(min(m, n)) memory. A table row depends only on the previous row. Keep two rows prev and cur of length n + 1 and swap them after every i. If you make b the shorter one (swapping the strings — LCS is symmetric), the memory is O(min(m, n)). The price: the string itself can no longer be recovered from two rows — that needs the whole table or the clever algorithm in “Deeper”.

Numbers: 1000 × 1000 int is 4 MB; 10⁴ × 10⁴ is 400 MB, and there two rows are the only option.
cards/6/q: LCS on two table rows returns 2 instead of 1 for a = “ba”, b = “aa”. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: Arrays are reference types: prev = cur doesn’t copy the row, it makes both variables the same array. From the second row on, prev[j − 1] is already the new value of the current row, and one “a” from a pairs with both “a”s of b. It needs a reference swap (prev, cur) = (cur, prev): the old prev becomes the buffer for the next row.
cards/7/title: Edit Distance: three operations — three neighbours
cards/7/body:
Edit Distance (LeetCode #72), strings up to 500 characters. What is the minimum number of operations “insert a character”, “delete a character”, “replace a character” that turns a into b? “horse” → “ros” takes 3: replace h with r (rorse), delete r (rose), delete e (ros). This is the Levenshtein distance.

State: dp[i, j] is the number of edits that turn a[..i] into b[..j]. Base: dp[i, 0] = i — delete everything, dp[0, j] = j — insert everything.

Transition on the last characters. Equal — no edit needed: dp[i − 1, j − 1]. Different — 1 + the best of three operations, each one a neighbour:

↖ replace a[i − 1] with b[j − 1]: what remains is prefixes i − 1 and j − 1.
↑ delete a[i − 1]: what remains is turning a[..i − 1] into b[..j].
← insert b[j − 1] at the end: what remains is turning a[..i] into b[..j − 1].

O(m·n) time, and the memory squeezes to two rows the same way. In a game: a developer console with fuzzy command search — “spwn” finds spawn, “godmod” finds godmode: the names closest by distance. 300 commands of 15 characters is about 7·10⁴ cells per keystroke — a fraction of a millisecond.
cards/8/task: Walk the Edit Distance table for “horse” → “ros”. Under each cell — which transition won. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes in.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: Cell (2, 2): “o” and “o”. Diagonal dp[1, 1] = 1, above dp[1, 2] = 2, left dp[2, 1] = 2. What goes in?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: The characters are equal — no edit needed, take the diagonal as it is: 1. “ho” → “ro” costs exactly as much as “h” → “r”, one replacement. Adding +1 on a match is a common mistake.
cards/8/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: 2: take the cell above, no edit needed
cards/8/goal/asks/1/q: The last cell (5, 3): “e” and “s”. Diagonal dp[4, 2] = 3, above dp[4, 3] = 2, left dp[5, 2] = 4. What goes in?
cards/8/goal/asks/1/explain: The characters differ: 1 + min(3, 2, 4) = 3, and the cell above won — deleting “e”. Above is “hors” → “ros”, 2 edits; plus deleting the last “e”. Only the diagonal comes for free, and only for equal characters.
cards/9/q: What is true about DP on two strings? Select all.
cards/9/options/0: Edit Distance takes the diagonal without + 1 when the characters are equal
cards/9/options/1: LCS on two table rows can return both the length and the subsequence itself
cards/9/options/2: The Edit Distance base is the first row 0, 1, 2, … and the first column 0, 1, 2, …
cards/9/options/3: Memory can be squeezed to O(min(m, n)) by making the inner-loop string the shorter one
cards/9/options/4: In LCS, equal characters require taking the maximum of three neighbours
cards/9/explain: Equal characters need no edit — the diagonal as it is. The base is “delete everything” and “insert everything”. A table row is as long as the inner-loop string, so that is the one to make short. Two rows give only the length: the walk back needs the whole table. In LCS a match only needs diagonal + 1 — it is never less than the neighbours, the character-swap argument proves it.
cards/10/q: You are solving Edit Distance out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: which operations and their cost? letter case? string lengths?
cards/10/items/1: Naively: enumerating edits is exponential, but a subproblem is a pair of prefixes
cards/10/items/2: The state dp[i, j] — edits for a[..i] → b[..j]; the base — i and j
cards/10/items/3: Transition: equal → diagonal, otherwise 1 + min(replace ↖, delete ↑, insert ←)
cards/10/items/4: Run a small example: “ab” → “b” — one deletion
cards/10/items/5: Complexity: O(m·n) time, memory down to two rows — O(min(m, n))
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: an empty string — the answer is the other’s length, equal strings — 0
cards/10/explain: The question about operation costs changes the transition (for example, a replacement costing 2), so it comes first. Explaining what each neighbour means matters more than writing the formula: the interviewer almost always asks “why is above a deletion?”.
cards/11/body:
Longest Common Substring — contiguous: on a match dp[i − 1, j − 1] + 1, on a mismatch 0 (the substring breaks), and the answer is the maximum over the whole table.

Longest Palindromic Subsequence (#516) is the LCS of a string and its reverse. Delete Operation for Two Strings (#583) is m + n − 2·LCS: everything outside the common part gets deleted. Shortest Common Supersequence (#1092) is m + n − LCS, and the string itself comes from a walk back over the LCS table.

Diff. Comparing two versions of a file is LCS over lines: lines outside the common subsequence are exactly the deleted and added ones. In a game — showing a designer the difference between two versions of a config, dialogues or a localization table.

Fuzzy search. In a developer console or an asset search you usually need not the exact distance but “at most k”: then cells further than k from the diagonal don’t need computing, and a row can stop as soon as its minimum exceeds k.
cards/11/deep:
Recovery in O(min) memory. The LCS string or the list of edits can be obtained without the full table: compute the two-row table down to the middle of a top-down, and for the reversed strings bottom-up, find the column where the sum is maximal (minimal for edits) — the point the optimal path passes through — and solve the two halves recursively. The time stays O(m·n) (about twice as much), the memory is O(m + n). This is the classic technique when you need the answer itself and the table doesn’t fit in memory.

A band. If you only need the answer when the distance is ≤ k, cells with |i − j| > k are certainly greater than k: compute a band of width 2k + 1, O(k·n) instead of O(m·n). For console suggestions k = 2–3.

Swapped neighbours. The most common typos are transposed letters (“spanw”). The Damerau–Levenshtein distance adds a fourth transition: if a[i − 1] == b[j − 2] and a[i − 2] == b[j − 1], then dp[i − 2, j − 2] + 1.

Faster than O(m·n). In the worst case you can’t do substantially better (there are conditional lower bounds), but in practice diff tools use algorithms that run in O((m + n)·D), where D is the number of differences: on almost identical files that is almost linear. There are also bit-parallel variants of LCS and Levenshtein: one machine operation processes 64 cells of a column.

.NET and Unity. int[,] checks two bounds on every access; a flat int[] indexed by i * (n + 1) + j, or two rows, is usually faster. For suggestions on every keystroke keep two rows in a field and reuse them — don’t allocate a table per command; for short strings stackalloc works. The LINQ on the card allocates delegates with a closure, iterators, a sort buffer and a list — fine for a console, not for per-frame code. Compare case-insensitively with char.ToLowerInvariant up front, once per string, not in every cell.
cards/12/q: Match the problem with its transition or formula.
